title: Loading an electric kiln for a glaze firing
subtitle: Kiln furniture placement, glaze-free foot rings, shelf spacing, and temperature ramp for a cone 6 (1220 degrees Celsius) glaze firing in an electric kiln
excerpt: Loading a kiln for a glaze firing is not simply stacking pots on shelves. Each piece must sit on a glaze-free foot ring, shelves must be spaced to allow heat circulation, kiln furniture must be stable, and the temperature ramp must suit the clay bodies and glazes being fired. A badly loaded glaze firing wastes a full kiln of work. A well-loaded one produces consistent results across every shelf.
sourceNotes: Electric kiln loading and glaze firing technique derived from first principles. Kiln furniture placement documented in Emmanuel Cooper, The Potter's Book of Glaze Recipes (2004, University of Pennsylvania Press). Temperature ramp guidance from Ceramic Frequency open-access technical notes.

glossaryTerms.definition: The shelves, posts, and props used to support pottery inside the kiln during firing
A mixture of alumina and silica painted onto kiln shelves to prevent glaze drips from bonding pots permanently to the shelf
The raised ridge at the base of a pot that it sits on; must be completely free of glaze before loading
A pyrometric device placed inside the kiln to verify that the correct heat-work has been achieved. Cone 6 bends and falls at approximately 1220 degrees Celsius.
The rate at which the kiln temperature is increased or decreased per hour, controlled by the kiln's electronic controller or by manual adjustment

content.text: Loading a kiln for a glaze firing is a skill that directly determines whether glazed work survives or is ruined. Every piece in the kiln needs a glaze-free
foot ring
, and every kiln shelf needs a coat of
kiln wash

as a second line of defence. Pieces that touch each other or the shelf with glaze will be fused together and destroy both the piece and the shelf. The guidance below covers a cone 6 (1220 degrees Celsius) glaze firing in a standard front-loading or top-loading electric kiln.

Heat in an electric kiln is not perfectly even. The top and bottom shelves run cooler than the middle shelves in many kilns. Knowing your kiln's hot and cool spots, found by firing test tiles in a witness firing, lets you place pieces that need the most consistent temperature in the middle of the load.

attrs.title: Studio safety
attrs.content: Silica dust is the chronic studio hazard. Silicosis is irreversible. Mix wet whenever possible. Wear a P100 respirator any time raw glaze powders are open. Wet-clean only: no sweeping, no compressed air, no dry sanding indoors. Ventilation matters: a downdraft vent or open window with an extractor. Wear welder's shade-5 glasses when peephole-watching at high temperatures. Never open a hot kiln below 80 degrees Celsius. Keep a Class A fire extinguisher within reach.

content.text: When to use this technique

Use this guidance for every cone 6 glaze firing in an electric kiln. The principles of shelf preparation, piece spacing, and temperature programming apply whether you are firing one shelf or a full load. The only variable is shelf count and post height, which adjust to suit the pieces being fired.
What you need

Kiln shelves matched to the internal diameter of your kiln. Full round or half-round shelves, or interlocking rectangular shelves. Kiln posts in at least two heights so you can vary shelf spacing to accommodate different piece heights. Kiln wash: a powder mixture of approximately 50 percent alumina hydrate and 50 percent silica, mixed with water to a paint consistency. A soft paintbrush for applying kiln wash. Bisque-fired, glazed pieces with clean foot rings. Pyrometric
cones
: a cone 5 guard cone (bends before target), a cone 6 target cone, and a cone 7 guard cone (bends after target), placed in a cone pack visible through the peephole.
Preparing and loading the kiln: step by step
Inspect all kiln shelves. Chip off any old glaze drips from previous firings. If bare shelf surface is visible, apply a fresh coat of
kiln wash
to those areas with the paintbrush. Allow to dry completely before loading. Never fire a shelf with wet kiln wash.
Inspect every glazed piece before loading. Check the
foot ring

and base of every piece: wipe away any glaze on the foot ring or within 5 mm of the base with a damp sponge. Glaze left on the foot ring will melt and bond the piece to the shelf. Run a finger over every foot ring: it should feel rough and matte, with no slippery glaze residue.
Plan the shelf arrangement before loading. Set
kiln furniture

posts at three or four points around each shelf, evenly spaced and matching in height. The posts carry the load of the next shelf and everything on it. Mismatched post heights cause shelves to tilt and pieces to slide.

Shelf spacing: add 20 to 30 mm clearance above the tallest piece on each shelf. This allows heat to circulate horizontally across the full width of the shelf. Pieces crowded against the shelf above them fire unevenly and can stick if a glaze runs.

Space pieces on each shelf: leave at least 15 mm between individual pieces. Pieces that touch during a glaze firing will fuse together permanently. Taller, narrower pieces can be placed near the kiln wall; wider, lower pieces in the centre where heat is more even.
Place a cone pack on the middle shelf at the peephole side of the kiln. The cone pack holds a
cone

5, cone 6, and cone 7 set in a small clay base at approximately 10 degrees off vertical. You can check the cone pack through the peephole during firing to confirm when cone 6 has bent to the correct angle.
Set the
temperature ramp

on the kiln controller: Segment 1: 60 degrees Celsius per hour to 120 degrees Celsius, hold 30 minutes (moisture drive). Segment 2: 100 degrees Celsius per hour to 600 degrees Celsius (quartz inversion zone, hold is optional). Segment 3: 150 degrees Celsius per hour to 1100 degrees Celsius. Segment 4: 60 degrees Celsius per hour to 1220 degrees Celsius (cone 6 target), hold 10 minutes. Switch off and allow the kiln to cool passively: do not open the lid or door until the kiln reads below 80 degrees Celsius.
What it looks like when it's right

After the kiln has cooled and you open it, every piece should sit cleanly on its own foot ring on the shelf, with no fusing to adjacent pieces or to the shelf surface. The glaze should be smooth and glossy (or matte, depending on the glaze), with no crawling or bare patches. The cone 6 witness cone in the cone pack should be bent to the standard position, approximately 40 degrees from the vertical.

Shelves that were properly coated with kiln wash allow any glaze drips to be chipped off cleanly without damaging the shelf. A shelf without kiln wash that has caught a glaze drip will typically be permanently contaminated at that spot and should be recoated on all surfaces before the next use.
Common mistakes

Missing glaze on the foot ring. The most common cause of pots fusing to shelves. Check every foot ring by touch before loading, not just by eye. Glaze residue is not always visible under studio lighting.

Uneven kiln post heights. A tilted shelf means that any glaze that runs during firing flows toward the low edge and onto adjacent pieces. Always measure post heights with calipers or match sets from the same batch.

Opening the kiln too hot. Thermal shock to pieces at over 100 degrees Celsius can cause crazing or cracking, particularly in thick-walled forms. Wait until the kiln reads below 80 degrees Celsius before opening.

Firing too fast through the quartz inversion zone at 573 degrees Celsius. All silica in the clay body undergoes a sudden volume change at this temperature. A too-fast ramp through this zone can cause pieces to crack. The 100 degrees Celsius per hour ramp in Segment 2 handles this safely.
